          f"task 2 at negative gains, max {neg2.max():.3f}, fraction >= 0.99: {np.mean(neg2 >= 0.99):.2f}, >0.8: {np.mean(neg2 > 0.8):.2f}")
    x = g / noise_l[nl]
    inplot = (x > 0) & (x <= 10)
    print(f"   within Figure 8B's plotted range (task signal / noise from 0 to 10, 8-1-model/main1.py set_xlim): "

          f"for task signal / noise >= 0.3: {np.mean(m.score1b[(x >= 0.3) & (x <= 10)] >= 0.99):.2f}")
    print("   task 1 by positive gain:", dict(zip(np.round(g[g > 0], 3)[::4].tolist(), np.round(pos1.to_numpy(), 3)[::4].tolist())))
for nl in range(len(noise_l)):

    print(f"   SNR {1 / noise_l[nl]:.4g}: best task 1 {m.score1b[g > 0].max():.3f}, best task 2 {m.score2b[g < 0].max():.3f}")

# Variants: the narrow linear gains (linspace -20 to 20), and the share of Figure 8B's positive
# axis (symlog, matplotlib's default linthresh 2, x from 0 to 10) where task 1 is at least 99%.
from matplotlib.scale import SymmetricalLogTransform
narrow = np.argsort(np.argsort(ggains))[80:]
pivn = sub_all[sub_all.ngain.isin(narrow)].groupby(["n_noise_level", "ngain", "nrep"])[["score1b", "score2b"]].mean() / 4.0 / NT
medn = pivn.groupby(["n_noise_level", "ngain"]).median()
tr = SymmetricalLogTransform(10, 2, 1)
for snr in [0.0625, 0.25]:
    nl = int(np.where(np.isclose(1 / noise_l, snr))[0][0])
    m = medn.loc[nl]; g = gains_l[m.index.to_numpy()]
    pos1 = m.score1b[g > 0]
    print(f"SNR {snr}, narrow gains: {int((g > 0).sum())} positive gains ({g[g > 0].min():.2f} to {g.max():.2f}, task signal / noise "
          f"{g[g > 0].min() / noise_l[nl]:.3f} to {g.max() / noise_l[nl]:.2f}); task 1 max {pos1.max():.3f}, fraction >= 0.99: "
          f"{np.mean(pos1 >= 0.99):.2f}, range {pos1.min():.3f} to {pos1.max():.3f}")
    print("   task 1 by positive gain:", dict(zip(np.round(g[g > 0], 2)[::4].tolist(), np.round(pos1.to_numpy(), 3)[::4].tolist())))
    # All positive gains of both ranges, sorted by task signal / noise, on the plotted axis
    mb = pd.concat([med.loc[nl], m]); gb = gains_l[mb.index.to_numpy()]; xb = gb / noise_l[nl]
    keep = (xb > 0) & (xb <= 10)
    order = np.argsort(xb[keep]); xs = xb[keep][order]; ok = (mb.score1b.to_numpy()[keep][order] >= 0.99)
    if not ok[-1]:
        print("   both ranges: task 1 is below 0.99 at the largest plotted x")
        continue
    first_ok_run = xs[np.where(~ok)[0].max() + 1] if (~ok).any() else xs[0]
    y0, y1, y10 = tr.transform([0.0, first_ok_run, 10.0])
    print(f"   both ranges: task 1 >= 0.99 at every sampled x from {first_ok_run:.3f} to 10; share of the positive plotted axis: "
          f"{(y10 - y1) / (y10 - y0):.2f}; share of the linear x range 0 to 10: {(10 - first_ok_run) / 10:.2f}")

Result: reproduced. With 320 neurons and an SNR of 0.0625 the best positive task signal gives 93.2% correct in both tasks, above 80%. At an SNR of 0.25 task 1 is at least 99% at every sampled task signal over noise from 0.32 to 10, which is 90% of Figure 8B's positive plotted axis (symlog) and 97% of the linear range 0 to 10, and at 38 of the 40 positive gains of the code's narrow linear sweep (95%). Within the plotted range it is below 99% only for task signals under 0.3 times the noise, where task 1 performance runs from about 0.63 at the smallest gains to 0.988 at a gain of 1.194 (task signal / noise 0.30); outside the plotted range it falls for gains of 84 and more (0.52 at 84). Counted over the code's log-spaced broad gains, which crowd near zero, only 25% of the positive gains reach 99% (30% within the plotted range). The outcome reads "most positive task signals" as most of the range of task signals the paper plots, which the narrow sweep confirms; counted per log-spaced sample the second part would not hold.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. Every analysis follows the paper's code at commit 390b608 where the claims file names it, ported to Python 3 (R's Mann-Whitney and signed-rank tests are reproduced with scipy's normal approximations with continuity correction; Benjamini-Hochberg with statsmodels; logistic regression with scikit-learn's liblinear solver and balanced class weights). The auditory response class and window come from the code's unit table (M4 reading (a)); recomputing them from the spikes as the Supplement describes (reading (b), a variant) gives 46 mPFC and 61 A1 responsive units in place of 31 and 49. Part of the difference comes from rules of the table that the paper does not state (units the table classes "too brief", "lasts too long" or "lasts to end" are responsive under reading (b)), and part from the threshold and trial choices of reading (b): 6 units the table classes "nothing" become responsive, and 13 the table counts as responsive (5 A1, 8 mPFC) are not responsive under reading (b). The single-unit onsets of Figure 5A and 5B match the paper only with the code's smoother, which moves each spike to the 50 ms sample grid; with exact spike times the mPFC median is 0.75 s. They also need the units whose bin just before onset is not significant to be kept, as main4.py keeps them; leaving them out gives 0.65 s in A1, and the outcome is marked as resting on this assumption. The latency difference of Figure S5E rests on the code's windows: recomputed windows give medians of 16.38 and 16.25 ms, which do not differ. The count of evoked changes beyond baseline matches only with the code's Benjamini-Hochberg correction. The model's second condition holds over the plotted range of task signals and the narrow linear sweep, not over the log-spaced samples counted one by one. Bootstrap and shuffle draws use fixed seeds of their own, so their p-values differ from the paper's draws by sampling error.

What was found about the data set. The spike files are pandas 0.10 pickles from Python 2 that current pandas cannot open, and they hold 2977 clusters of which only the 220 well-sorted units listed in the code's table were analysed: without that table the units, their quality and their auditory response windows cannot be identified from the data set. Three sessions have no spike file (their klusters0/ holds a README), and two CR21A sessions carry a second spike file outside klusters0/ with the same spike times but tetrode groups numbered 0 to 7 and different unit numbers. The descriptor names the stimulus column stimulus_name (it is stim_name) and gives a stimulus numbering that the files do not follow. The code's figure index names the units of Figures 4A and 4B the other way round from the legends; after a reader's answer the claims file identifies them by preference, as the legends do.
